title: Lena and the House
premise: Theo Thackeray, a pest controller with a habit of documenting everything, is called to a house where something leaves fingerprints at ceiling height and every mirror runs one second behind reality. As she investigates, she uncovers that the house feeds on what its residents love most, and that in 1974 the family who lived there buried something in the well to buy their survival. The house has chosen Theo as its next tenant, and the only way out is to return what was taken before the well refills on the winter solstice. She succeeds, but the price is that she must leave behind the one person she came to love inside the house's walls.
about_author: Dominic Thackeray is the pen name of a former building surveyor who spent a decade inspecting derelict properties across northern England and never quite got over the houses that felt like they were watching back. This is a second novel, written in a converted mill flat with the mirrors covered.

chapters.title: Call-Out
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Theo arrives at a decaying house on Fenwick Lane for a routine infestation call, finding no pests but fingerprints pressed into the plaster nine feet up, too large and too many-jointed. She documents everything, as she always does, because documentation is a kind of prayer. The beat is professional unease curdling into fascination.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Working alone overnight, Theo notices the hallway mirror reflecting the room a full second late, then the bathroom mirror, then a framed photograph's glass. She films it, and the footage shows the reflection moving before she does. The beat is the collapse of her rational framework and the first thrill of being truly seen by a place.

chapters.title: The 1974 File
chapters.summary: POV Theo, with interleaved documents. In the county archive Theo finds the house's history: the Aldous family, a child's disappearance never solved, and a well sealed by court order in 1974. She meets Marlow, the archivist who has his own history with the house, and their cautious alliance begins. The beat is the comfort of research becoming compulsion.

chapters.title: What the House Wants
chapters.summary: POV Theo. The house begins accommodating her: doors open before she reaches them, a kettle she never bought appears, her name is spelled in dust. The horror is hospitality. Marlow warns her that the house is courting her the way it courted the Aldouses. The beat is the seduction of belonging she never had anywhere else.

chapters.title: The Well Lid
chapters.summary: POV Theo and Marlow in alternating sections. They pry open the sealed well and find it dry, lined with handprints from the inside, and at the bottom a child's tin box containing a wedding ring and a confession letter dated three days before the disappearance. The beat is dread hardening into purpose: something was taken, and something was traded.

chapters.title: Refilling
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Water begins rising in the dry well with no source, and the reflections in the mirrors start showing a room that isn't hers, furnished in 1970s style, with a small figure standing in the corner. The fingerprints climb lower down the walls each night. Theo realizes the solstice deadline is real. The beat is time pressure transforming curiosity into fear.

chapters.title: Marlow's Debt
chapters.summary: POV Marlow. Marlow confesses he grew up in the house's shadow: his mother was the Aldouses' neighbor and took the tin box from the well as a child, which is why his family survived when others on the lane did not. The house has been waiting for its property to come home. The beat is guilt, and Theo's realization that love and duty point in opposite directions.

chapters.title: The Second Room
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Following the figure in the mirrors, Theo finds the 1970s room rendered physically behind the cellar wall: the missing Aldous child, unaged, kept as the house's heart, holding the ring's pair. The child asks her, in a voice like well-water, whether she would trade someone she loved to live. The beat is the book's moral crux made flesh.

chapters.title: Solstice
chapters.summary: POV Theo. On the solstice night, with the well brimming and the house sealing its doors, Theo descends with the tin box and the ring, intending to return what was taken and free the child. The house offers her a bargain: stay, belong, be loved forever, and the child stays too. She chooses to break the trade instead, giving the house herself as witness, its missing piece, in exchange for the child's release. The beat is sacrifice disguised as a transaction.

chapters.title: Documentation
chapters.summary: POV Marlow, then Theo's final recorded entry. Marlow finds the house empty, the mirrors exact, the well sealed with fresh mortar, and Theo's notebook complete to the last page. The final entry, dated the solstice, is written in her hand but describes the house from the inside. The beat is grief braided with peace: she paid the price of survival by refusing it, and the house finally has someone who chose to belong.
